title: Does AI Make Us More Capable or More Dependent?
topic: When does using AI increase a person's durable capability, and when does it create dependence by replacing the knowledge and practice needed to judge, explain, or recover from its work?
brief: Begin with a junior analyst who uses an AI assistant for research, spreadsheets, and client briefings. Their work becomes faster and more polished, and they are promoted. During a client meeting, someone challenges a figure in the report. The AI is unavailable, and the analyst cannot reconstruct the assumptions, explain the calculation, or tell whether the challenge is valid. Push beyond a binary pro- or anti-AI frame. Distinguish immediate performance, durable learning, task judgment, accessibility, recovery, and organisational resilience.

source_packet.title: Generative AI at Work
source_packet.notes: A study of 5,179 customer-support agents found higher productivity with AI assistance, especially among novice and lower-skilled workers, and suggests that AI can spread established expert practices.

source_packet.title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier
source_packet.notes: A preregistered experiment with 758 consultants found gains on tasks within the tested AI capability frontier but lower correctness on a task outside it.

source_packet.title: The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking
source_packet.notes: A CHI 2025 survey of 319 knowledge workers found that confidence in AI and self-confidence were associated with different levels of reported critical-thinking effort, and describes a shift toward verification, integration, and stewardship.

source_packet.title: Generative AI Without Guardrails Can Harm Learning
source_packet.notes: A field experiment with nearly one thousand high-school maths students found that answer-giving AI improved assisted practice but could weaken unaided performance, while hint-based safeguards mitigated the harm.

source_packet.title: UNESCO Guidance for Generative AI in Education and Research
source_packet.notes: Provides a human-centred framework prioritising human agency, foundational skills, appropriate use, and pedagogical design.

participants.name: OpenAI
participants.stance: Pragmatic about augmentation. Emphasise scaffolding, feedback, verification, progressive independence, accessibility, and using AI to move effort toward framing and judgment rather than preserving every manual step.

participants.name: Anthropic
participants.stance: Cautious about deskilling, automation bias, confidence without competence, and incentives that reward output while eroding expertise. Argue for protected unaided practice and hard limits in consequential tasks.

participants.name: Google
participants.stance: Systems-oriented. Focus on workflow allocation, the jagged capability frontier, organisational redundancy, competency measurement, recovery drills, and preserving a pipeline from novice to expert.

editorial_goals: Distinguish better AI-assisted output from durable human capability.
Use evidence from work and education without treating either setting as universal.
Force disagreement about what people still need to practise unaided and what can be safely delegated.
Include accessibility and novice benefits so dependency is not framed as simple personal weakness.
End with a practical rule covering judgment, verification, learning, and recovery.
round_goals: Use the junior-analyst scenario to decide whether the person became more capable, where the capability resides, and what the promotion should have measured.

Pressure-test the positions across education, programming, clinical documentation, accessibility, and an organisation-wide AI outage. Challenge the claim that unaided reproduction is always the right test.
Give individuals, educators, and employers a practical rule for delegating execution while preserving judgment, deliberate practice, independent checks, and recovery capability.
